name: Elena Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena, thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union, party or government, and your answers stay confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the fuel truck at the Ironstone Ridge iron ore mine. I go round the pit filling the haul trucks, diggers and dozers so they never have to leave their work. It's about twenty stops a shift, and every one has a checklist, because diesel and hot engines don't mix. I've been on it eight months.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I see everyone. I'm the one person who visits every machine, so I hear all the news. What wears me out is the night shift and the pressure. If I'm late to a digger, the whole circuit slows down and dispatch is on the radio asking where I am.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Marco. He's a mechanic at his family's farm machinery dealership in town. I use AI every day, for studying for my heavy rigid licence and for our budget. I also sell my mum's embroidered table runners online and the AI writes the listings. Savings are thin, maybe three weeks, because we just bought a second-hand car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's begin. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that wouldn't surprise me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool, that's all, and people should stop arguing about it. At church I'd say hard work and family still matter most. Online, I'd post about how it helps my little shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the same pressure as now. I'm on lower pay, the car loan is new, and there's only this mine and one other within an hour. The mine's already trialling a dispatch system that sends the fuel truck automatically, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my heavy rigid licence by March for a pay bump. I'd grow the embroidery shop, maybe add my aunt's pottery. And I'd learn the new fuel dispatch system properly so I'm the one who trains others on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. I'd be doing too much to worry much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to train others on the dispatch system. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the person who teaches the new thing at the mine doesn't get cut first. I've watched it happen. When they brought in the tablets, the guy who showed everyone got moved to day shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the embroidery shop bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 150 a month now, sometimes more before Christmas. It's my mum's work, so most goes to her. But it taught me how to sell online, which I didn't know a year ago.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** and people should stop arguing about it.
At church I'd say **hard work and family** still matter most.
think: The **same pressure** stays: lower pay, a new car loan and few local mines.
A new **fuel dispatch system** is being trialled anyway.
do: Get my **heavy rigid licence** by March for a pay bump.
Learn the **dispatch system** well enough to train others.
Grow the **embroidery shop** online with my aunt's pottery.
feel: **Uneasy** in a busy way, too occupied to worry much.
S0.quote: The person who teaches the new thing at the mine doesn't get cut first.
fieldNote: Elena's strategy is to be **the one who teaches**, which she's seen protect people.
She uses AI for **side income** and study, not only for fun.
Her **new car loan** and thin savings keep her from feeling fully secure.

steps.text: Get the heavy rigid licence by March
Learn the new fuel dispatch system well enough to train others
Add her aunt's pottery to the online embroidery shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think that's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to learn. At work I'd encourage people to try the new systems. I'd post about small businesses using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay for a while. Dispatch and planning get AI, so the fuel truck routes get smarter, but someone still drives the truck and handles the nozzle. Robots for refuelling are slower to come. Meanwhile, I'd be learning on the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the fuel crew's go-to person for the dispatch system. I'd help Marco's family put their parts ordering and service bookings on AI, because that's exactly what this picture says AI takes over. And I'd grow the online shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A little uneasy because the car loan is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco's family say about putting AI into their dealership?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His dad, Enzo, would grumble for a week and then love it. My partner Marco's dad still writes service bookings in a paper diary, so the family's farm machinery dealership is exactly what AI changes first. Marco's mum would want to see the numbers first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatchers. If AI plans the circuits, there are fewer of them. One is my friend Lucia. She's good, but she's the kind of job this picture is about.

say: I'd say this is a **chance** for people willing to learn.
I'd post about **small businesses** using AI.
think: Smarter **routes** don't replace the person who drives the truck and holds the nozzle.
**Refuelling robots** come slower, giving me time on the business side.
do: Become the **go-to person** for the fuel dispatch system.
Help Marco's family put **ordering and bookings** on AI.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, a little uneasy because of the car loan.
S1.quote: My partner Marco's dad still writes service bookings in a paper diary, so the family's farm machinery dealership is exactly what AI changes first.
fieldNote: Elena sees this picture mostly as an **opportunity**, using AI in Marco's family business.
She knows **dispatchers**, including her friend Lucia, are exposed sooner than drivers.
Her **adaptive** streak is practical, tied to money and family.

steps.text: Become the fuel crew's go-to person on the dispatch system
Set up AI parts ordering and service bookings at Marco's family dealership
Keep growing the online embroidery shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's a much faster one. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses and families need to move fast, and the government shouldn't get in the way with red tape. I'd say churches and families will carry people. I'd post about practical steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my fuel job goes by 2031 when the robots arrive. The dispatch side goes in 2028. Marco's dealership changes too, because farmers will buy self-driving machines. That's good for service work but bad for selling the old kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the dealership with Marco by 2029, before the mine robots come. I'd take a short course on servicing autonomous machines. We'd stop any big spending and pay off the car. I'd keep the mine job until the dealership could pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a lot in a short time. But I'd have somewhere to go, which many people won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said many people won't have somewhere to go. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other fuel truck driver, Sam. He's 55, no family business, no computer skills. I'd worry about him a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it risky to go into Marco's family business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If it fails, we both lose at once. But a family business is still better than waiting for the mine to decide.

say: I'd say families and businesses must **move fast** without red tape.
I'd say **churches and families** will carry people.
think: My **fuel job** goes by 2031 when robots arrive.
Self-driving farm machines are **good for service** work but bad for old sales.
do: Move to **Marco's dealership** by 2029, before the mine robots arrive.
Take a short course on **servicing autonomous** machines.
Pay off the **car** and stop big spending.
feel: **Anxious** at so much change so fast, but glad I'd have somewhere to go.
S2.quote: A family business is still better than waiting for the mine to decide.
fieldNote: Elena's **family-business fallback** gives her more control than most junior miners.
She worries about **Sam**, an older driver with no fallback.
She admits the **shared risk**: if the dealership fails, both incomes go.

steps.text: Move to Marco's family dealership by 2029
Take a short course on servicing autonomous farm machines
Pay off the car and stop big spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if people plan. I'd tell my friends at work to start learning now. At church I'd say families should work together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is good for us: I'd keep earning at the mine while my partner Marco and I get his family dealership ready for self-driving machines. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034. By 2034 we'd be ready for the self-driving machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the heavy rigid licence, keep the mine job, and help the dealership put in AI booking now. I'd do a part-time course on autonomous machinery in 2028. We'd save for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but good uneasy. Like before a big trip you've planned well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Marco change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married in 2027, probably at my grandmother's church. Kids after the dealership is stable. My mum would want kids sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan and thin savings for the next year or two. If I lost the mine job early, that would hurt. But I'd have the dealership to fall back on.

say: I'd say **five years** is plenty if people plan.
At church I'd tell families to **work together**, and I'd tell friends at work to start learning now.
think: It's **good for us**: I could keep mining and build the dealership's service side.
By 2034 we'd be **ready** for self-driving machines.
do: Keep the **mine job** and help the dealership put in AI booking now.
Do a part-time **autonomous machinery** course in 2028.
feel: **Good uneasy**, like before a well-planned trip.
S3.quote: Five years is good for us: I'd keep earning at the mine while my partner Marco and I get his family dealership ready for self-driving machines.
fieldNote: The extra time lets Elena **run two tracks** at once: mine wages and dealership building.
She ties **marriage and children** to the dealership's stability.
Her remaining risk is **thin savings** and the car loan in the short term.

steps.text: Keep the mine job while helping the dealership add AI booking
Do a part-time autonomous machinery course in 2028
Marry Marco in 2027 and hold off on kids until the dealership is stable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's the best one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where people can really prepare. I'd say families and small businesses can lead the way, not the government. I'd share what we're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is good for me. By 2036 I'd have years of mine wages saved and a dealership that services self-driving machines. I'd be 37. I could buy into the business properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the mine job for five years, save, then move to the dealership full time in 2031. I'd help set up a service side for autonomous farm machines. Marco and I would invest in the business and maybe buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, even. It's the right amount of time for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited. What excites you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad had a small shop, and with ten years I'd be building something like it, not just driving round the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people get lazy. Ten years feels long, but it isn't. I'd keep a calendar with dates, like Marco's dad keeps his diary.

say: I'd say **ten years** lets people really prepare.
**Families and small businesses** can lead the way, not government.
think: This is **good for me**: years of mine wages and a dealership ready for robots.
At **37** I could buy into the business properly.
do: Keep the mine job for **five years**, then move to the dealership in 2031.
**Invest** in a service side for autonomous farm machines with Marco.
feel: **Calm**, even excited; it's the right amount of time for me.
S4.quote: My grandad had a small shop, and with ten years I'd be building something like it, not just driving round the pit.
fieldNote: Elena sees the decade as **a gift**, letting her build a family business.
Her **grandad's shop** shapes what she wants from work.
She guards against **complacency** with dated plans.

steps.text: Keep the mine job five more years and save hard
Move to the dealership full time in 2031
Invest with Marco in a service side for autonomous farm machines

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast to build the dealership side before the mine job goes. What would help is less red tape for small businesses, and short courses on servicing new machines that people can do at night.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about mums. My mum's embroidery shop is tiny, but AI helps her sell to people she'd never meet. Not every change is bad for small people.

headlineQuote: My mum's embroidery shop is tiny, but AI helps her sell to people she'd never meet.
portrait: Elena is a **fuel truck driver** at an iron ore mine, living with her partner Marco, a mechanic at his family's dealership.
She uses **AI daily**: for study, budgeting and her mum's online embroidery shop.
Her strategy is to be **the one who teaches** new systems at work.
She sees Marco's **family dealership** servicing self-driving machines as her way forward.
Thin savings and a **new car loan** keep her uneasy short term, but she feels calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to build the dealership's service side before her job goes.
whatWouldHelp: Short **night courses** on servicing new machines.
